finding, preserve the authoritative invention, strengthen the figure brief, and regenerate the
sheet from the authoritative text until the pixels conform. A stubborn rendering artifact remains
a drawing defect; it does not become part of the invention.

For a figure-plan coverage failure, never delete a disclosed part, numeral definition, or
supporting specification text. Redistribute labels among focused sheets, or add a focused sheet
when necessary, and synchronize the drawing descriptions.

If a figure brief is over-specified, shorten it by removing invented rendering constraints while
preserving the authoritative text, numeral table, disclosed geometry, and required relationships.
Replace generic negative linework controls with positive descriptions of the required bodies,
edges, contacts, openings, and paths. Do not ban second boundaries, parallel lines, inner lines,
rims, ledges, or chamfers merely to suppress a prior rendering artifact.
Remove generic face-linework controls such as prescribing one stroke for every outline or a
shared edge drawn once. Keep only the positive physical geometry and relationship.
For an endpoint finding, choose a broad interior target on the intended part whenever possible.
Remove exact midpoint, depth, quarter, or toward-an-end modifiers that are not disclosure-grounded
or necessary to distinguish the intended part. Replace ordinal geometry references with explicit
outermost, middle, innermost, left, or right terms whenever the order could be read in more than
one direction.

26	- **[critical] Exclusive assertion that the jaw carriages are the only parts touching the pipe is untraced** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶7 ("Overall arrangement"); draft/06-summary.md ¶5) - The description asserts an exclusivity relationship (nothing but the carriages contacts the pipe) and a negative structural fact (no frame bore contact), and the Summary repeats it. The disclosure never says the jaw pads are the sole contact members or that the frame bore stands clear of the pipe; it says only that each carriage carries a pad that bears on the pipe without requiring a tool-specific diameter. No affirmative USER passage supports the exclusivity or the bore/no-bore relationship. The sentence also mis-attributes contact to the carriages when the description and claim 1 put the contact on the pivoting jaw pad 40 carried by the carriage.
27	  - Suggested fix: In ¶7 replace the quoted sentence with: "The jaw pads carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped." In draft/06-summary.md ¶5 replace "The frame therefore takes up its position on the pipe from the jaws rather than from a bore matched to a nominal pipe size, and the pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter." with "The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter."

The disclosure identifies the part only as "a follower" received in the oblique slot and gives it no form.
31	  - Suggested fix: Replace the sentence with: "The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34." (FIG. 3 may keep its generic post outline, which is a permitted depiction convention, so long as the text asserts no form.)
32	- **[critical] FIG. 2 depicts an overlapping stepped lap joint at both cam-ring joints; the joint topology is untraced** (figures/fig-02.md, "Geometry and relationships" ¶3–¶4) - The brief specifies a particular joint topology: each segment end is stepped so that the outer part of one segment and the inner part of the other reach past the joint in opposite senses, meeting along two circumferentially facing surfaces. An interdigitated lap joint conveys technical substance (radial interlock at the joint, force transfer in both circumferential senses through overlapping tongues) that the disclosure never provides. Calling it "drawn schematically" does not convert it into a permitted convention, because it adds a structural relationship rather than merely choosing an outline. A plain abutting pair of circumferentially facing end surfaces is the shape-neutral choice and is fully consistent with the description's characterization of the faces.
33	  - Suggested fix: In fig-02.md replace both joint paragraphs with: "At the left joint the two segment ends meet along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially, one on the end of the first cam ring segment 22 and one on the end of the second cam ring segment 24. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26." and the corresponding sentence for the right joint and numeral 28. Make no change to the description or claims, which are already shape-neutral.
34	- **[critical] FIG. 4 specifies a count of four dished (Belleville) washers for the force-limiting spring stack** (figures/fig-04.md, "Geometry and relationships" ¶4) - The brief fixes both the element count (four) and the element type (dished washers / disc springs in a chevron section) for the force-limiting spring stack. Counts and element form are technical substance, not depiction convention. The disclosure names only "a force-limiting spring stack", and the description deliberately keeps it generic ("one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack"), so the figure is more specific than both the source and the text it illustrates.
35	  - Suggested fix: In fig-04.md replace the sentence with: "To the right of that block, a compression spring is drawn schematically as a zigzag line running from the upright right face of the wedge 52 to a flat plate at the right end. The disclosure says only that the wedge is driven "against a drive face of the cam ring" and gives the face no carrier, form, or position.
37	  - Suggested fix: In fig-02.md replace the lug paragraph with: "A short circumferentially facing surface is formed on the second cam ring segment 24 near the right joint. That surface is the ring drive face 36." In fig-04.md replace the lug sentence with: "The right end of the band terminates in a flat surface facing right; that surface is the ring drive face 36," and update the numeral targets in both briefs to point at that surface. Leave the description unchanged; it already says only that the face "faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it."

The disclosure states only that a spring biases each carriage outward and says nothing about the spring's type or where it seats. FIG. 3 must show the spring somewhere, and its ledge/flange arrangement is an acceptable depiction convention, but the application text may not convert that renderer's choice into an asserted structure and connection.
39	  - Suggested fix: Replace the sentence with: "The carriage return spring 44 acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge the jaw carriage 30 radially outward." In ¶55 correspondingly replace "may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that" with "may act at any location on the jaw carriage 30, provided that".
40	- **[major] Mounting boss placement freedom and "a bracket" in the supported-equipment list are untraced** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶9) - Two additions. First, the description enlarges the disclosed list of carried equipment with "a bracket" and "other equipment"; the disclosure lists only a sensor, tool, or conduit (and the claims correctly recite only those three, so the description is broader than both the source and the claims). Second, the description asserts that the boss may be placed on either frame half at any circumferential position - a positional variant the disclosure never grants; it says only that the frame may carry the boss outside the annular guide.
41	  - Suggested fix: In ¶9 change the first quoted sentence to: "The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100." Delete the clause ", and the mounting boss 70 may be placed on either frame half at whatever circumferential position suits the equipment to be carried", ending that sentence after "the jaws are advanced."
42	- **[major] Self-centering result claimed and stated as an express limitation without an affirmative source passage** (draft/09-claims.md claim 8; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶29 last sentence; draft/05-background.md ¶7) - Claim 8 recites the centering of the frame on the pipe as an express result limitation, and the description and Background bridge paragraph repeat it. The disclosure never states that the clamp centers itself, finds the pipe center, or is self-centering; it states synchronized inward travel of the three carriages and independence from a tool-specific pipe diameter. Centering may well follow geometrically from equal synchronized advance of three distributed jaws, but there is no affirmative inventor passage stating the result, and the working title in brief.md ("Self-Centering...") is authority for the title only, never for technical invention matter. The title itself may stand as filed.

In Background ¶7 replace "so that the clamp finds the center of the pipe by itself over a range of pipe sizes" with "so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes". Retain the title as given in the brief.

FIG. 3 is sectioned in a plane containing the radial direction and the frame axis with radially outward toward the top, and shows the slot as an opening passing through the ring "from top to bottom", i.e. from the radially inner face to the radially outer face, dividing the ring section into left and right portions and receiving a post that rises radially from the jaw carriage. An axial through-slot cannot be entered by a radially rising post, and in the FIG. 3 section plane an axial slot would appear as a void running left-to-right at one radial level rather than as a top-to-bottom opening. The two briefs cannot both be rendered. The disclosure fixes neither orientation ("a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring"), so either may be chosen, but one must be chosen consistently.
45	  - Suggested fix: Adopt the FIG. 2 orientation (axial through-slot) and conform FIG. 3. In fig-03.md ¶3 replace the last two sentences with: "It is interrupted at its middle by a rectangular opening passing through it from left to right, so that a radially outer portion and a radially inner portion of its outline remain above and below the opening. That opening is the oblique slot 34." In fig-03.md ¶5 replace "A short post rises from its upper end into the opening in the segmented cam ring 20, its sides facing the sides of that opening." with "A short post extends from its upper end into the opening in the segmented cam ring 20, its sides facing the radially outer and radially inner sides of that opening." Adjust the numeral 32 and 34 targets accordingly.
46	- **[major] FIG. 3 shows the annular guide open radially outward with clearance at each side, contradicting the stated retention of the cam ring** (figures/fig-03.md ¶3; draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶25; draft/09-claims.md claim 10) - The description and claim 10 require the annular guide to retain the cam ring against radial (and, in the description, axial) displacement while permitting circumferential movement. FIG. 3 shows the guide as a recess "open toward the top", and in that view radially outward is toward the top, so nothing retains the ring radially outward; it further shows the ring "narrower than the recess so that a clear space remains at each side of it", so nothing retains it axially either. As drawn, the ring would simply lift out of the frame.
47	  - Suggested fix: In fig-03.md ¶3 replace the first two sentences with: "The upper opening is a rectangular groove, wider than deep, formed in the body and closed on its radially outer side, the groove opening toward the left of the view through a mouth narrower than the groove so that a lip overhangs the groove on the radially outer side. That groove is the annular guide 18." and replace "narrower than the recess so that a clear space remains at each side of it" with "filling the groove in the radial direction and retained in it by the lip, a small running clearance remaining at each side". # Previous review - verdict: fail

Reviewed disclosure.md, conversation.md (which restates the disclosure verbatim and adds no further USER matter), brief.md, draft sections 01–10, numerals.md, and figures/fig-01.md through fig-04.md. The core architecture of the draft traces cleanly to the inventor's words: split semicircular frame halves with hinge and releasable latch, three radial jaw carriages in radial guides with pivoting concave pads, a two-segment cam ring in an annular guide with complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends that couple on closing, followers in oblique slots producing synchronized inward travel, a latch-driven wedge acting on a ring drive face through a limited stroke, carriage return springs, the two latch positions, the force-limiting spring stack between handle and wedge, the indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing over a predetermined compression range, the non-participating mounting boss, and the install/remove sequence. Formalities check out: title matches the brief, no priority claim, no government support, abstract is under 150 words, no drafting notes or placeholders remain, all 25 numerals are unique and each appears in at least one figure brief. The problems are (a) a set of specific structures, materials, counts, variants, and results in the description and figure briefs that have no affirmative passage anywhere in the disclosure or conversation, and (b) three verifiable geometric contradictions among FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and the description text concerning slot orientation, ring retention, and the wedge/drive-face interface. Fifteen findings follow, each with the candidate wording, the nearest source passage, and a filing-clean fix.

## Mechanical checks that did not pass

- **Source fidelity is clean before rendering** (fail): Reviewed disclosure.md, conversation.md (which restates the disclosure verbatim and adds no further USER matter), brief.md, draft sections 01–10, numerals.md, and figures/fig-01.md through fig-04.md. Formalities check out: title matches the brief, no priority claim, no government support, abstract is under 150 words, no drafting notes or placeholders remain, all 25 numerals are unique and each appears in at least one figure brief. The problems are (a) a set of specific structures, materials, counts, variants, and results in the description and figure briefs that have no affirmative passage anywhere in the disclosure or conversation, and (b) three verifiable geometric contradictions among FIG. 2, FIG. 3, FIG. 4, and the description text concerning slot orientation, ring retention, and the wedge/drive-face interface. Fifteen findings follow, each with the candidate wording, the nearest source passage, and a filing-clean fix.
  - Exclusive assertion that the jaw carriages are the only parts touching the pipe is untraced
  - Jaw pad facing/lining material and softer-than-pipe material are untraced
  - Follower embodied as pin, post, roller, or like projection is untraced
  - FIG. 2 depicts an overlapping stepped lap joint at both cam-ring joints; the joint topology is untraced
  - FIG. 4 specifies a count of four dished (Belleville) washers for the force-limiting spring stack
  - Ring drive face depicted on a discrete radially projecting lug
  - Carriage return spring seating (abutment and shoulder) asserted in the description is untraced
  - Mounting boss placement freedom and "a bracket" in the supported-equipment list are untraced
  - Self-centering result claimed and stated as an express limitation without an affirmative source passage
  - FIG. 2 and FIG. 3 depict the oblique slot in mutually incompatible orientations
  - FIG. 3 shows the annular guide open radially outward with clearance at each side, contradicting the stated retention of the cam ring
  - FIG. 4 wedge/drive-face interface is self-contradictory and inconsistent with the described wedging action

## Reviewer findings

- **[critical] Exclusive assertion that the jaw carriages are the only parts touching the pipe is untraced** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶7 ("Overall arrangement"); draft/06-summary.md ¶5) - The description asserts an exclusivity relationship (nothing but the carriages contacts the pipe) and a negative structural fact (no frame bore contact), and the Summary repeats it. The disclosure never says the jaw pads are the sole contact members or that the frame bore stands clear of the pipe; it says only that each carriage carries a pad that bears on the pipe without requiring a tool-specific diameter. No affirmative USER passage supports the exclusivity or the bore/no-bore relationship. The sentence also mis-attributes contact to the carriages when the description and claim 1 put the contact on the pivoting jaw pad 40 carried by the carriage.
  - Suggested fix: In ¶7 replace the quoted sentence with: "The jaw pads carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped." In draft/06-summary.md ¶5 replace "The frame therefore takes up its position on the pipe from the jaws rather than from a bore matched to a nominal pipe size, and the pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter." with "The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter."
- **[critical] Jaw pad facing/lining material and softer-than-pipe material are untraced** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶31 ("The jaw carriages"), last sentence) - The description adds a material variant for the bearing face, including a comparative hardness relationship and named pipe conditions (coated, thin walled). The disclosure says nothing about pad materials, facings, or liners. Coated and thin-walled pipe appear only in the Background as prior-art context, which cannot support invention text.
  - Suggested fix: Delete the sentence from ¶31 in its entirety. No replacement text is needed; the preceding sentences already state the disclosed function of the concave pivoting face.
- **[critical] Follower embodied as pin, post, roller, or like projection is untraced** (draft/08-detailed-description.md ¶27 ("The jaw carriages"), last sentence) - The description offers four alternative embodiments of the follower. Calling it "drawn schematically" does not convert it into a permitted convention, because it adds a structural relationship rather than merely choosing an outline. 1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and presents a concave pad face at its inner end, the pad being described below in connection with FIG. 3. The three jaw carriages 30 are the only members of the clamp 100 that touch the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped, and the position of the frame on the pipe 90 is established by them rather than by contact between the pipe 90 and a bore of the frame. The clamp 100 accordingly does not require a frame bore, liner, or insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide described below. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, a bracket, a length of conduit, or other equipment that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced, and the mounting boss 70 may be placed on either frame half at whatever circumferential position suits the equipment to be carried. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.
18	
19	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end.
22	
23	The jaw carriages
24	
25	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form an annular guide 18 that receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The annular guide 18 is formed in both frame halves, one arcuate portion of the annular guide 18 in each frame half, and the two arcuate portions register with one another in the closed condition to form a continuous annular path in which the coupled ring turns.
26	
27	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 may be a pin, a post, a roller, or a like projection able to bear against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
28	
29	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together and the frame takes up a position centered on the pipe.
30	
31	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required. The bearing face may be faced or lined with a material chosen for the pipe to be gripped, for example a material softer than the pipe surface where a coated or thin walled pipe is to be clamped.
32	
33	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 and biases the jaw carriage 30 radially outward. In the illustrated embodiment the carriage return spring 44 is a compression spring seated between an abutment of the radial guide 38 and a shoulder of the jaw carriage 30. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. The jaws are thus retracted from the pipe by the same synchronized path, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.
34	
35	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
36	
37	FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
38	
39	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44 and the clamp 100 can still be slid or turned along the pipe 90 to its intended position. In a second, over-center position, the latch handle 50 has been carried past the point of maximum resistance, and the reaction transmitted back from the wedge 52 through the force-limiting spring stack 54 acts to hold the latch handle 50 in the second position rather than to open it, so that the latch 16 stays closed without a separate securing element. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.
40	
41	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.
42	
43	An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, at the clamp itself and without any separate instrument, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90 and is not derived from the position of the jaw carriages 30: a large pipe and a small pipe seat the jaw pads 40 at different points in the stroke of the coupled ring, but the indicator pin 56 shows the same predetermined compression range in each case when the same clamping force has been reached.
44	
45	Operation
46	
47	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
48	
49	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping and can still be positioned along the pipe 90. When the clamp 100 is where it is wanted, the operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
50	
51	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, turning the coupled ring back through its stroke by way of the followers 32 in the oblique slots 34, so that all three jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90 together. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
52	
53	Variations
54	
55	The frame halves, the segmented cam ring 20, the jaw carriages 30, and the latch 16 may be made of any materials having the strength and stiffness required for the loads to be carried, and the parts that slide on one another, in particular the segmented cam ring 20 in the annular guide 18 and each jaw carriage 30 in its radial guide 38, may be surfaced or lubricated to reduce friction in the drive path. The hinge 14 may be any joint that allows the frame halves to swing apart about a fixed axis at the hinge end while holding the complementary coupling faces 26 in register when the halves are closed. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 may take any complementary shapes that transmit circumferential force between the segments and that come into engagement as the frame halves close and separate as they open. The wedge 52 may act on the ring drive face 36 directly or through an intermediate sliding member, provided that the force-limiting spring stack 54 remains in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The carriage return spring 44 of each jaw carriage 30 may act between the jaw carriage 30 and its radial guide 38 as illustrated, or elsewhere on the jaw carriage 30, provided that it biases the jaw carriage 30 outward when the drive from the latch 16 is removed.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition and with which the axis of a clamped pipe substantially coincides, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and presents a concave pad face at its inner end, the pad being described below in connection with FIG. 3. The three jaw carriages 30 are the only members of the clamp 100 that touch the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped, and the position of the frame on the pipe 90 is established by them rather than by contact between the pipe 90 and a bore of the frame. The clamp 100 accordingly does not require a frame bore, liner, or insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide described below. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, a bracket, a length of conduit, or other equipment that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced, and the mounting boss 70 may be placed on either frame half at whatever circumferential position suits the equipment to be carried. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 faces circumferentially and is presented at a position on the ring where the latch can reach it, in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end.

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30. The frame is channeled to form an annular guide 18 that receives the segmented cam ring 20 and retains it against radial and axial displacement while permitting it to move circumferentially. The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

lines: Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken automatically with each use and requires no separate assembly step.

-The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that circumferential movement of the ring produces a radial displacement of anything constrained to follow the slot. The three oblique slots 34 have the same inclination, so that a given rotation of the coupled ring advances each jaw carriage 30 by the same radial increment. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30, and is selected so that the available stroke of the coupled ring produces the radial travel required to span the intended range of pipe diameters, and so that the mechanical advantage at the jaw pads 40 is sufficient for the clamping force to be developed by hand at the latch 16. A shallower inclination gives greater mechanical advantage and less radial travel for a given stroke, and a steeper inclination gives more radial travel and less mechanical advantage.

+The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 confines the follower 32 to a path that is inclined to the radial direction. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in slots of the same inclination in one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism, by equal radial increments, for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads therefore close on the pipe together and the frame takes up a position centered on the pipe.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands, and the contact is distributed along the face instead of being taken at one edge of it. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required. The bearing face may be faced or lined with a material chosen for the pipe to be gripped, for example a material softer than the pipe surface where a coated or thin walled pipe is to be clamped.

A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 and biases the jaw carriage 30 radially outward. In the illustrated embodiment the carriage return spring 44 is a compression spring seated between an abutment of the radial guide 38 and a shoulder of the jaw carriage 30. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward, the followers 32 bear on the opposite sides of their oblique slots 34, and the coupled ring is turned back through its stroke. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 also clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart, so that the pipe surface is not scraped by a jaw pad 40 that is still bearing on it.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Here the force-limiting spring stack 54 is the most compliant element of the drive train once the jaw pads 40 are seated. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others, and the clamping force delivered at the jaw pads 40 is accordingly determined by the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than by how hard the operator pulls the latch handle 50. The force-limiting spring stack 54 comprises one or more resilient elements arranged in a stack whose combined rate and travel are chosen so that the stack is stiff enough to carry the load required to advance the jaw carriages 30 to the pipe 90, and yielding enough to absorb the remaining travel of the latch handle 50 over the intended range of pipe diameters.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is made continuous again by the act of closing the clamp, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch toward a closed position rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The frame therefore takes up its position on the pipe from the jaws rather than from a bore matched to a nominal pipe size, and the pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss being connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.

A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.

Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.

What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself restored to a single, continuous element by the act of closing the clamp, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the clamp finds the center of the pipe by itself over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.

# FIG. 1

## View
Plan view of the assembled split pipe clamp, closed around a pipe, viewed along the axis of the pipe. Black line work on white, no shading, no hatching, all of it well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A circle at the centre of the drawing area is the pipe 90, seen end on.

A ring of substantial width surrounds the pipe 90, drawn as an inner circular boundary and an outer circular boundary. The inner boundary is spaced outward from the pipe 90, leaving a visible gap between them.

Two radial joint lines divide the ring into two semicircular bodies, one joint at the left of the ring and one at the right of the ring. The upper semicircular body is the first frame half 10 and the lower semicircular body is the second frame half 12.

At the left joint is the hinge 14, drawn schematically as a small circle centred on that joint line with a short knuckle block reaching to it from each frame end.

At the right joint is the latch 16, drawn schematically as a rectangular block lying outside the outer boundary of the ring and bridging both frame ends, with an elongated lever extending from the block alongside the outer boundary of the second frame half 12.

Three jaw carriages 30 are spaced around the ring, one at the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right. Each is drawn as a block that crosses the inner boundary of the ring and reaches radially inward toward the pipe 90. The topmost jaw carriage lies on the first frame half 10; the other two lie on the second frame half 12.

Each jaw carriage 30 carries at its inner end a separate member, joined to the jaw carriage 30 at a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. The inner face of that member is a shallow concave arc that meets the outer surface of the pipe 90. That member is the jaw pad 40.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 100 split pipe clamp: target the outer boundary of the ring in the upper right region.
- 10 first frame half: target well inside the upper semicircular body, between its boundaries, right of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 12 second frame half: target well inside the lower semicircular body, between its boundaries, at the bottom of the ring.
- 14 hinge: target the small circle at the left joint.
- 16 latch: target the rectangular block bridging the right joint.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the block of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the member at the inner end of the topmost jaw carriage.
- 90 pipe: target well inside the central circle.

# FIG. 2

## View
Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, all of it well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by an inner circular boundary and an outer circular boundary, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside the inner boundary is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing the radial direction of that jaw carriage and the axis of the frame. Radially outward is toward the top of the view, and the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, all of it well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view. A groove is formed in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, and the two meet.

The groove is wider than it is deep, is bounded by the body on its radially outer side above and its radially inner side below, is closed at its right, and opens toward the left of the view. A lip projects downward from the radially outer wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across the mouth, leaving the rest of the mouth open. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it in the radial direction with a small running clearance at the walls above and below, and held in the groove by the lip. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. It is interrupted by a rectangular opening that passes through it from left to right, so that a radially outer portion of its outline remains above the opening and a radially inner portion remains below the opening. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward through the body from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38. A ledge projects into the channel from its left wall near the lower end.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from the upper end of that block, passes through the open part of the mouth and enters the opening in the segmented cam ring 20, its upper and lower sides facing the radially outer and radially inner sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A flange projects from the left side of the jaw carriage 30 above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body is carried on the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 through a small circle centred on the joint between them, the circle being a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc opening downward.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 18 annular guide: target the wall of the groove above the block that lies in it.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target well inside the hatching of the block in the groove, above the opening.
- 30 jaw carriage: target well inside the hatching of the block in the channel, below the flange.
- 32 follower: target well inside the post.
- 34 oblique slot: target the open space of the opening, to the right of the post.
- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel, below the mouth of the groove.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the lowest body, above its concave lower face.
- 44 carriage return spring: target the zigzag line.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, viewed as in FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, all of it well inside the drawing area.

At the lower left of the drawing area a plain hatched body in section carries the parts shown. A shallow open channel in its upper face holds a hatched arcuate band that runs from the left edge of the view toward the middle. That band is the segmented cam ring 20. Near the right end of the band, its upper side runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants downward toward the right. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure in section stands on the plain body, with a left wall, a right wall and a top wall around an interior cavity, the cavity opening downward at the bottom of the enclosure above the right end of the band. That enclosure is the latch housing 58.

A block lies in the lower part of the cavity between the left and right walls, which guide it to move up and down in the view. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears against it, so that downward movement of the block drives the band to the left. That block is the wedge 52.

Above that block, within the cavity, a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line running from the upper face of the wedge 52 up to a flat plate lying across the cavity. That spring is the force-limiting spring stack 54.

An elongated lever is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle in the upper right part of the cavity and extends upward and to the right, passing out above the right wall and ending well inside the drawing area. A short link joins the lever to the flat plate, so that the lever presses the plate downward. The lever leans to the right, past the upright, in the over-centre position. That lever is the latch handle 50.

A slender pin rises from the flat plate, passes through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above that top wall. That pin is the indicator pin 56.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing the radial direction of that jaw carriage and the axis of the frame. Radially outward is toward the top, and the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above on its radially outer side and below on its radially inner side, closed at its right, and open toward the left. A lip projects downward from the radially outer wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it, leaving the rest of the mouth open. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance at the walls above and below and held in by the lip. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, so that a radially outer portion of its outline remains above the opening and a radially inner portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38, and a ledge projects into it from its left wall near the lower end.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the open part of the mouth and into the opening in the segmented cam ring 20, its upper and lower sides facing the radially outer and radially inner sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A flange projects from the left side of the jaw carriage 30 above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body is carried on the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 through a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc opening downward.

- 18 annular guide: target the wall of the groove above the block lying in it.

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing the radial direction of that jaw carriage and the axis of the frame. Radially outward is toward the top, and the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above on its radially outer side and below on its radially inner side, closed at its right, and open toward the left. A lip projects downward from the radially outer wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it, leaving the rest of the mouth open. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance at the walls above and below and held in by the lip. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, so that a radially outer portion of its outline remains above the opening and a radially inner portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38, and a ledge projects into it from its left wall near the lower end.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the open part of the mouth and into the opening in the segmented cam ring 20, its upper and lower sides facing the radially outer and radially inner sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A flange projects from the left side of the jaw carriage 30 above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body is carried on the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 through a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc opening downward.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left. A lip projects downward from the upper wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it, leaving the rest of the mouth open. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below and held in by the lip. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, leaving a portion of its outline above the opening and a portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38, and a ledge projects into it from its left wall near the lower end.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the open part of the mouth and into the opening in the block above, its upper and lower sides facing the radially outer and radially inner sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A flange on the left side of the jaw carriage 30 stands above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc opening downward.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, viewed as in FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top of the view and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, all of it well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
At the lower left of the drawing area a plain hatched body in section carries the parts shown. A shallow open channel in its upper face holds a hatched arcuate band that runs from the left edge of the view toward the middle. That band is the segmented cam ring 20. Near the right end of the band, its upper side runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants downward toward the right. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure in section stands on the plain body, with a left wall, a right wall and a top wall around an interior cavity, the cavity opening downward at the bottom of the enclosure above the right end of the band. That enclosure is the latch housing 58.

A block lies in the lower part of the cavity between the left and right walls, which guide it to move up and down in the view. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears against it, so that downward movement of the block drives the band to the left. That block is the wedge 52.

Above that block, within the cavity, a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line running from the upper face of the wedge 52 up to a flat plate lying across the cavity. That spring is the force-limiting spring stack 54.

An elongated lever is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle in the upper right part of the cavity and extends upward and to the right, passing out above the right wall and ending well inside the drawing area. A short link joins the lever to the flat plate, so that the lever presses the plate downward. The lever leans to the right, past the upright, in the over-centre position. That lever is the latch handle 50.

A slender pin rises from the flat plate, passes through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above that top wall. That pin is the indicator pin 56.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 16 latch: target the outer boundary of the enclosure at its lower right corner.
- 20 segmented cam ring: target well inside the hatching of the arcuate band, near the left edge of the view.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the upper side of the band, where the block bears on it.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the lever, above the top wall of the enclosure.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the lower part of the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line above that block.
- 56 indicator pin: target the part of the pin standing above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target well inside the hatching of the top wall of the enclosure.

Part names above are semantic identifiers only; the image carries no text, numerals, or labels.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left. A lip projects downward from the upper wall at the mouth of the groove and reaches part way across it, leaving the rest of the mouth open. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below and held in by the lip. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, leaving a portion of its outline above the opening and a portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38, and a ledge projects into it from its left wall near the lower end.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the open part of the mouth and into the opening in the block above, its upper and lower sides facing the radially outer and radially inner sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A flange on the left side of the jaw carriage 30 stands above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.
