# FIG. 2

## View
Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, all of it well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by an inner circular boundary and an outer circular boundary, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside the inner boundary is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the two segment ends meet along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially, one surface on the end of the first cam ring segment 22 and one on the end of the second cam ring segment 24. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints. Each is an oblique slot 34, drawn as a long narrow opening with rounded ends, lying within the width of the annulus and clearly inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end of the slot is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary.
Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants inward as it approaches that joint, so that the segment is shallower at the joint than a short distance away from it. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right region.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment, in its upper left region.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment, at the bottom of the annulus.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the meeting surfaces at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top of the annulus.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface on the outer boundary near the right joint.

# FIG. 2

## View
Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside the inner boundary is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the two segment ends meet along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially, one surface on the end of the first cam ring segment 22 and one on the end of the second cam ring segment 24. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints. Each is an oblique slot 34, drawn as a long narrow opening with rounded ends, lying within the width of the annulus and clearly inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end of the slot is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary.
Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants inward as it approaches that joint, so that the segment is shallower at the joint than a short distance away from it. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Deleted the clause assigning the ring drive face to a particular cam ring segment from the detailed description, so the text now says only that the face is presented where the wedge can reach it and lies at an inclination to the wedge's advance. Deleted the vestigial "Variations" heading and the duplicated spring-stack sentence, leaving the closing paragraph as the end of the description. Fixed the inclination sense of the oblique slots in the FIG. 2 brief so the drawing agrees with the drive direction FIG. 4 fixes: in each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary, so clockwise rotation, the sense the wedge drives in FIG. 4, brings the inner portion of each slot to the station held by its outer portion. reasoning: The segment-identity clause was deleted outright rather than reworded. The disclosure names only a drive face of the cam ring, so the specification now carries no statement about which segment holds it; the placement of numeral 36 on the second cam ring segment stays confined to the FIG. 2 brief as a depiction convention, and the FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 briefs were not changed on that point.

Claim support was checked before deleting the Variations sentence: the force-limiting spring stack is still recited as lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52 in the latch paragraph, which is what claims 2, 12 and 15 need, so the deletion removed a duplicate and not a support passage. No substitute variant material was added.

The FIG. 2 slot sense was derived from the geometry already fixed elsewhere rather than invented. FIG. 4 has the wedge descending on the ring drive face and driving the band away from the latch joint; on the lower segment in FIG. 2 that direction is clockwise. Under clockwise rotation the material presented at a fixed circumferential station is the material lying counterclockwise of it, so the inner end of each slot must lie counterclockwise of the outer end for the carriages to advance inwardly as claim 1 and the description require.
The added sentence describes the slot geometry and the rotation sense only, without naming the follower, because numeral 32 is not listed on the FIG. 2 sheet and the followers are not drawn there.

The FIG. 2 brief was shortened at the view line, the annulus sentence, the hinge-end joint sentence, the drive face sentence and two numeral targets so that adding the inclination sense kept the file under the character limit; every trim removed wording, not geometry or a relationship.

Deleted the vestigial "Variations" heading and the duplicated spring-stack sentence, leaving the closing paragraph as the end of the description. Fixed the inclination sense of the oblique slots in the FIG. 2 brief so the drawing agrees with the drive direction FIG. 4 fixes: in each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary, so clockwise rotation, the sense the wedge drives in FIG. 4, brings the inner portion of each slot to the station held by its outer portion. Trimmed wording elsewhere in the FIG. 2 brief to keep it under the character limit.
reasoning: The segment-identity clause was deleted outright rather than reworded. The disclosure names only a drive face of the cam ring, so the specification now carries no statement about which segment holds it; the placement of numeral 36 on the second cam ring segment stays confined to the FIG. 2 brief as a depiction convention, and the FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 briefs were not changed on that point.

Claim support was checked before deleting the Variations sentence: the force-limiting spring stack is still recited as lying in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52 in the latch paragraph, which is what claims 2, 12 and 15 need, so the deletion removed a duplicate and not a support passage. No substitute variant material was added.

The FIG. 2 slot sense was derived from the geometry already fixed elsewhere rather than invented. FIG. 4 has the wedge descending on the ring drive face and driving the band away from the latch joint; on the lower segment in FIG. 2 that direction is clockwise. Under clockwise rotation the material presented at a fixed circumferential station is the material lying counterclockwise of it, so the inner end of each slot must lie counterclockwise of the outer end for the carriages to advance inwardly as claim 1 and the description require.
The added sentence describes the slot geometry and the rotation sense only, without naming the follower, because numeral 32 is not listed on the FIG. 2 sheet and the followers are not drawn there.

The FIG. 2 brief was shortened at the view line, the annulus sentence, the hinge-end joint sentence, the drive face sentence and two numeral targets so that adding the inclination sense kept the file under the character limit; every trim removed wording, not geometry or a relationship.

All 25 numerals still appear in the description, the five sheets still carry 8, 7, 8, 8 and 3 numerals with names identical to the table, and no claim, numeral definition, or disclosed embodiment changed in this pass.
changes: draft/08-detailed-description.md: deleted ", in the illustrated embodiment on the segment adjacent the latch end," from the ring drive face sentence.

draft/08-detailed-description.md: deleted the "Variations" heading and the duplicated sentence placing the force-limiting spring stack between the latch handle and the wedge; the paragraph beginning "Features described above" now closes the description.

figures/fig-02.md: added the inclination sense to the oblique slot paragraph, tying it to the clockwise drive direction fixed by FIG. 4; restored the paragraph break before the ring drive face paragraph; shortened the view line, the annulus sentence, the hinge-end joint sentence, the drive face sentence and the numeral targets for 20 and 34 to stay within the character limit.
data.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md is still empty, so the Background cites nothing and characterizes no document. This pass changed no claim and removed no supporting text: claim 1 continues to rest on the cam ring divided between the frame halves and re-coupled at the hinge end and the latch end by the closing motion, so that one latch input rotates a single coupled ring and advances all three jaw carriages through their oblique slots in synchronism. The dependent ladder is unchanged, including the force-limiting spring stack and the indicator pin that reports stack compression rather than pipe diameter, the two latch positions, the pivoting concave pad that needs no size-specific insert, the arcuate guide portions, the coupling faces that separate with the halves, and the isolated mounting boss carried into independent claim 11. That is the sense required by claim 1 and by the description's statement that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of the jaw carriages.
- The paragraph break before the ring drive face paragraph was restored, and wording was trimmed at several points so the brief stays under the character limit (now 2797 characters).

No claim, numeral definition, or disclosed embodiment changed. Sheet numeral counts remain 8, 7, 8, 8 and 3; all 25 numerals still appear in the description and on at least one sheet; all five briefs are under the limit; and no notes, placeholders or em dashes remain.

3	Traced every claim limitation, numbered part, and figure-brief structure against input/disclosure.md and the single USER passage in input/conversation.md (which is verbatim identical to the disclosure). The substantive ledger is almost entirely clean: the frame halves, hinge, latch, three radial jaw carriages with pivoting concave jaw pads, the segmented cam ring in the annular guide with one segment per half, the complementary coupling faces at both ends, followers in oblique slots, the wedge acting on a ring drive face, the carriage return springs, the two latch positions, the force-limiting spring stack, the indicator pin against a fixed edge of the latch housing, the mounting boss, and the install/remove method all trace to exact affirmative inventor sentences. No drafting notes, placeholders, open questions, or unresolved alternatives remain, and the numerals table is complete, gap-free in meaning, and used consistently in the description. Six problems require correction before render: a geometric contradiction between the FIG. 4 view convention and the drive sense asserted in FIG. 2 (and the handle direction in FIG. 1); a description clause that makes the ring stroke a fixed quantity, which contradicts the spring-stack behavior and the variable-diameter premise; an unanchored claim term ("closed position" of the latch) that collides with the "first position" of claim 5 and appears nowhere in the description; independent claims 1, 11 and 14 omitting the force-limiting spring stack that the inventor expressly names as part of "the disclosed essential relationship"; a numeral in FIG. 4 that points at the structure already designated by another numeral; and an unsupported ledge-and-flange spring-seat arrangement in the FIG. 3 brief. Each has a filing-clean fix confined to the file where the problem occurs.

6

8	  - FIG. 4's stated view convention makes the wedge rotate the ring in the direction opposite to the drive sense asserted in FIG. 2, and opposite to FIG. 1's handle direction
9	  - Description makes the cam-ring stroke a fixed quantity set by latch travel, contradicting the spring-stack behavior and the variable-diameter premise

16	
17	- **[major] FIG. 4's stated view convention makes the wedge rotate the ring in the direction opposite to the drive sense asserted in FIG. 2, and opposite to FIG. 1's handle direction** (figures/fig-04.md (View section and wedge paragraph), read against figures/fig-02.md (slot inclination and ring drive fa) - FIG. 4 fixes its orientation as a non-mirrored view of FIG. 1 ("viewed as in FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top"). In FIG. 1 and FIG. 2 the latch joint is at the right of the ring (3 o'clock), where clockwise circumferential motion points downward; rotating that region so radially outward points up puts clockwise motion toward the RIGHT of the view. FIG. 4 nevertheless has the wedge drive the band to the LEFT, i.e. counterclockwise, while FIG. 2 states that clockwise is "the sense in which the wedge drives it in FIG. 4" and inclines the slots so that only clockwise rotation advances the carriages inwardly. Two further consequences confirm the mismatch: under the non-mirrored reading the segment lying to the left of the latch joint would be the first cam ring segment 22, whereas FIG. 2 places the ring drive face 36 on the second cam ring segment 24; and FIG. 1 requires the lever to stand "on the side of the block remote from the second frame half 12" (upward in FIG. 1), which the non-mirrored reading maps to the left of FIG. 4, while FIG. 4 has the lever "lean right". Every one of these three discrepancies disappears if FIG. 4 is taken from the opposite axial side, so the defect is confined to the one phrase that declares the viewing direction. Nothing in draft/07-drawings.md or draft/08-detailed-description.md states a viewing direction for FIG. 4, so the correction stays inside the figure brief.
18	  - Suggested fix: In figures/fig-04.md, replace the clause "viewed as in FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right" with "taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies circumferentially toward the first frame half 10". Leave every other sentence of figures/fig-04.md, and all of figures/fig-01.md and figures/fig-02.md, unchanged.

The two statements cannot both hold; as written the description asserts a fixed ring stroke while also asserting that the ring stops where the pipe stops it. The inventor's only statement on the point is that the ring turns "through a limited stroke", i.e. an upper bound, not a fixed value.
20	  - Suggested fix: In draft/08-detailed-description.md, replace "the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the extent of the stroke being set by the travel of the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16." with "the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the stroke being limited by the travel available to the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16."

Nothing in the disclosure names a latch "closed position"; the inventor names only the holding position and the over-center position.
22	  - Suggested fix: In draft/09-claims.md claim 1, replace "such that movement of the latch toward a closed position drives the wedge against the ring drive face and rotates the coupled ring through the stroke" with "such that movement of the latch drives the wedge against the ring drive face and rotates the coupled ring through the stroke". In draft/06-summary.md, replace "so that movement of the latch toward a closed position rotates the coupled ring through the stroke" with "so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke".
23	- **[major] All three independent claims omit the force-limiting spring stack that the inventor identifies as part of the disclosed essential relationship** (draft/09-claims.md, claims 1, 11 and 14) - The disclosure closes by naming four things as "the disclosed essential relationship": closure couples the ring segments; latch travel drives the coupled ring; the oblique slots synchronize the radial jaw carriages; and the force-limiting spring stack accommodates the remaining latch travel. Claims 1, 11 and 14 recite the first three and omit the fourth, leaving the spring stack only in dependent claims 2, 12 and 15. On this record the independent claims cover an embodiment with a rigid drive train, which the description itself says drives one jaw farther into the pipe than the others and which the inventor never disclosed as an embodiment. This is a scope-versus-source mismatch, not a patentability opinion.
24	  - Suggested fix: In draft/09-claims.md: (a) add to claim 1, after the wedge element, "the latch comprising a latch handle and a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge, the force-limiting spring stack being arranged such that travel of the latch handle after all three jaw pads have contacted a pipe received in the frame compresses the force-limiting spring stack rather than advancing one of the jaw carriages farther inwardly than the others;" and amend claim 2 to read "The split pipe clamp of claim 1, wherein the latch further comprises a latch housing and an indicator pin coupled to the force-limiting spring stack, the indicator pin being movable relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range.", renumbering the remaining dependent claims and their references so that former claim 4 depends on the new claim 2; (b) add the same force-limiting spring stack limitation to the clamp recitation of claim 11 and amend claim 12 correspondingly; (c) add to claim 14, as a step after "moving the latch to a second, over-center position", "continuing to move a latch handle of the latch into the second position after all three jaw pads have seated on the pipe, thereby compressing a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge rather than advancing one of the jaw carriages farther inwardly than the others;" and amend claim 15 to depend on claim 14 reciting only the observation-free remainder, e.g. delete claim 15 and renumber claims 16 and 17 to depend on claim 14.
25	- **[minor] In FIG. 4 numeral 16 is targeted at the same enclosure outline that numeral 58 designates** (figures/fig-04.md, "Numerals on this sheet" list, entries for 16 and 58) - Numeral 16 (latch) is aimed at "the outer boundary of the enclosure at its lower right corner" and numeral 58 (latch housing) at "the hatching of the top wall of the enclosure". FIG. 1 already carries 16 for the latch as a whole.
26	  - Suggested fix: In figures/fig-04.md, replace the entry "- 16 latch: target the outer boundary of the enclosure at its lower right corner." with "- 16 latch: place in free space to the lower right of the enclosure, with its leader ending at a point in the empty space beside the enclosure and the handle, so that it designates the latch assembly as a whole and not the wall designated 58."
27	- **[minor] FIG. 3 brief adds a ledge on the radial guide wall and a flange on the jaw carriage as spring seats, which the inventor never described** (figures/fig-03.md, radial guide paragraph and carriage return spring paragraph) - The inventor discloses only that "A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released", and the description keeps this neutral ("acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame"). Locating a seat on one particular wall of the radial guide and one particular side of the carriage is a connection and relative-location choice that carries technical substance, so the schematic label does not cover it. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke, the stroke being limited by the travel available to the wedge 52 between the first and second positions of the latch 16.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is made continuous again by the act of closing the clamp, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch toward a closed position rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss being connected neither to the segmented cam ring nor to any jaw carriage, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies circumferentially toward the first frame half 10. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The flat plate is a spring seat shown schematically.

## Geometry and relationships
At the lower left a plain hatched body in section carries the parts shown. A shallow open channel in its upper face holds a hatched arcuate band running from the left edge of the view toward the middle. That band is the segmented cam ring 20. Near the right end of the band, its upper side runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants downward toward the right. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure in section stands on the plain body, with a left wall, a right wall and a top wall around a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band. That enclosure is the latch housing 58.

A block lies in the lower cavity between the left and right walls, which guide it up and down. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears against it, so that downward movement of the block drives the band to the left. That block is the wedge 52.

Above that block, a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the upper face of the wedge 52 to a flat plate lying across the cavity. That spring is the force-limiting spring stack 54.

An elongated lever is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle in the upper right of the cavity and extends upward and to the right, passing out above the right wall and ending well inside the drawing area. The lever bears directly on the flat plate and presses it downward. The lever leans right, past the upright, in the over-centre position. That lever is the latch handle 50.

A slender pin rises from the flat plate, through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58, and stands above it. That pin is the indicator pin 56.

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, leaving a portion of its outline above the opening and a portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38, and a ledge projects into it from its left wall near the lower end.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the mouth of the groove and into the opening in the block lying in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A flange on the left side of the jaw carriage 30 stands above the ledge, and a compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line from the underside of the flange down to the ledge. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

input.summary: Fixed all six findings. FIG. 4 is now expressly taken from the axial side opposite FIG. 1, so its leftward wedge drive is the clockwise sense FIG. 2 states and the lever leaning right matches the FIG. 1 handle direction. The description no longer makes the ring stroke a fixed quantity; the stroke is limited by the travel available to the wedge between the two latch positions. Claim 1 and the summary no longer use a latch "closed position", so nothing collides with the first position of the two-position latch claim. The force-limiting spring stack is now recited in all three independent claims, with the dependents restructured and renumbered to 15 claims. Numeral 16 in FIG. 4 now designates the latch assembly in free space beside the enclosure rather than the housing wall that 58 designates. The drive-direction chain is internally consistent across FIG. 1, FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 (slot inclination, clockwise ring rotation, wedge-on-drive-face sense, mirrored FIG. 4 view all reconcile), and both coupling-face pairs are load-bearing in opposite senses (drive via hinge-end faces, retraction via latch-end faces), so no logical gap there. Numerals are one-to-one and every numeral is used in both text and at least one sheet. No drafting notes, placeholders, or unresolved alternatives remain. - **[major] Claim 6 and description divide the annular guide into an arcuate portion in each frame half; the source never says the guide is so divided** (draft/09-claims.md claim 6; draft/08-detailed-description.md paragraph beginning "FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view) - Claim 6 recites a structural subdivision of the annular guide, and the description mirrors it. The inventor states only that the ring is "retained in an annular guide of the frame" and that "One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half." There is no affirmative passage describing the guide as two arcuate portions, one per half, each independently receiving and retaining its own segment while permitting that segment's circumferential movement. lines: Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

-The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 passes through the segmented cam ring 20 and is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

+The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

# FIG. 2

## View
Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside the inner boundary is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints. Each is an oblique slot 34, drawn as a long narrow opening with rounded ends, lying within the width of the annulus and clearly inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end of the slot is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary, as viewed in this figure, so that clockwise rotation of the ring, the sense in which the wedge drives it in FIG. 4, brings the inner portion of each slot to the circumferential position held by its outer portion.

Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants inward toward that joint. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment, in its upper left region.

- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.

# FIG. 2

## View
Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside the inner boundary is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the end of the first cam ring segment 22 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 meet along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along plain complementary surfaces that face circumferentially. Those surfaces are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints. Each is an oblique slot 34, drawn as a long narrow opening with rounded ends, lying within the width of the annulus and clearly inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end of the slot is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary, as viewed in this figure, so that clockwise rotation of the ring, the sense in which the wedge drives it in FIG. 4, brings the inner portion of each slot to the circumferential position held by its outer portion.

Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs for a short distance as a straight surface that slants inward toward that joint. That slanting surface is the ring drive face 36.

# FIG. 3

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The carriage return spring and its seats are shown schematically.

## Geometry and relationships
A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left portion, the two meeting.

The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. A rectangular opening passes through the block from left to right, leaving a portion of its outline above the opening and a portion below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34.

The channel runs downward from the mouth of the groove and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the mouth of the groove and into the opening in the block lying in the groove, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of that opening. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring is drawn as a zigzag line acting between the jaw carriage 30 and the wall of the channel so as to urge the jaw carriage 30 upward, that is, radially outward; its seats are shown schematically. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle that is a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 18 annular guide: target the groove wall above the block lying in it.

- 38 radial guide: target the right wall of the channel, below the groove mouth.
- 40 jaw pad: target well inside the lowest body.

# FIG. 4

## View
Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies circumferentially toward the first frame half 10, which lies outside this view. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. The flat plate is a spring seat shown schematically.

## Geometry and relationships
At the lower left a plain hatched body in section carries the parts shown; a shallow channel in its upper face holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle. Near its right end the upper side of the band runs as a short straight surface slanting downward to the right, the ring drive face 36.

To the right, a hatched enclosure in section stands on the plain body, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward above the right end of the band. That enclosure is the latch housing 58.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in the lower cavity between the left and right walls, which guide it up and down. Its lower left face slants at the same angle as the ring drive face 36 and bears on it, so downward movement of the wedge 52 drives the band to the left.

Above it, the force-limiting spring stack 54 is drawn as a zigzag compression spring line from the upper face of the wedge 52 to a flat plate across the cavity.

An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle in the upper right of the cavity and extends up and to the right, passing out above the right wall and ending inside the drawing area. It bears on the flat plate and presses it downward, leaning right, past the upright, in the over-centre position.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the flat plate through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it.

# FIG. 2

## View
Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the axis of the ring. Black line work on white, no shading, well inside the drawing area.

## Geometry and relationships
A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area, bounded by inner and outer circular boundaries, is the segmented cam ring 20. The space inside the inner boundary is empty.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments. The upper segment is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower segment is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet along plain complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, along plain complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings pass through the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left and one at the lower right, spaced from one another and from both joints; those circumferential positions are shown schematically. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening with rounded ends, lying within the width of the annulus and clearly inclined to the radius at its own position, so that one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer boundary. In each slot the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary, as viewed here, so that clockwise rotation of the ring, the sense in which the wedge drives it in FIG. 4, brings the inner portion of each slot to the circumferential position held by its outer portion.

Near the right joint, the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24 runs as a short straight surface slanting inward toward that joint, the ring drive face 36. The segment on which the ring drive face 36 is shown, and its position on the outer boundary, are shown schematically.

## Numerals on this sheet
- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary of the annulus in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment, in its upper left.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment, at the bottom of the annulus.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the meeting surfaces at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the slanting surface near the right joint.

Enlarged fragmentary section of the latch, taken at the latch end and viewed along the axis of the frame from the side opposite that of FIG. 1, so that radially outward is toward the top, the circumferential direction runs left to right, and the right of the view lies circumferentially toward the first frame half 10, which lies outside this view. The description no longer says the oblique slots pass through the ring, and the through-opening stays a rendering convention with its depth marked schematic in FIG. 3. reasoning: Claim 6 was recast to the retention relationship the disclosure supplies, that the ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame and one segment is carried by each frame half, rather than a guide divided into two arcuate portions each independently receiving its own segment. The description was changed in the same words so the claim has verbatim support, and the sentence about registering portions forming a continuous path is gone.

The through-slot assertion was deleted from the description so the text says only that each slot is inclined and drives its carriage inward. The opening still has to be drawn, so FIG. 3 now marks the depth of the opening schematic, which keeps the topology choice inside the brief where it belongs.

Three depiction choices that a drawing cannot avoid are now labeled as such in the briefs and nowhere else: which segment carries the ring drive face and where on the outer boundary it sits, the circumferential stations of the three slots, and the circumferential stations of the three carriages with their apportionment between the halves. The description and claims were left untouched on all three points, since they already speak only of a drive face on the ring and carriages distributed around the frame.

The FIG. 4 cross-section conflict was resolved with the broken-away convention rather than by relieving the outer wall of the guide, because relieving that wall at the latch end would be structure the disclosure never gives.
